title: Authorization models: RBAC, ABAC and ReBAC
subtitle: Roles, attributes and relationships. Pick a permission model that still works when your product grows.

c.v: npm is a package registry for JavaScript code. On 2 November 2021, GitHub, which runs npm, got a report through its bug bounty program.
The report showed that an attacker could publish new versions of any npm package from an account without proper
authorization
. GitHub patched it within six hours.
The cause was not a missing check. The check existed. The npm registry ran on several
microservices
. The authorization service checked the user's rights for the package named in the request URL.

But the service that wrote to the registry did not read the URL. It chose the package from the contents of the uploaded file. So a request could be authorized for one package and then applied to a different one.

GitHub fixed it by making both services use the same package for the check and for the publish. Its telemetry went back only to September 2020. The bug was older than that. For that window, GitHub said "with high confidence" that it was not exploited maliciously.

The lesson for this page: an authorization check is only as good as its model and its placement. You must check the right object, in the right place, with rules that match how the product shares things.
The
Authentication and authorization
lesson showed one check: "Does this order belong to this user?" Real products need more. People share folders, become members of teams, and become admins of a whole company account.
There are three common ways to model this.
RBAC
(role-based access control).
Permissions belong to roles. Users get roles. "Editors may edit docs."
ABAC
(attribute-based access control).
A policy reads facts about the user, the object, the action and the environment. "Users in finance may read invoices during work hours."
ReBAC
(relationship-based access control).
Access comes from links between users and objects. "You may view this doc because you are in a group that can view its folder."
Most real systems mix them. Roles for staff tools, relationships for sharing, and a few attribute rules on top.
The key idea.
Choose the model that matches how your product shares things. Then put the check in one place, on the server, for the exact object the action will touch.
RBAC: users, roles, permissions
In RBAC, each user gets one or more roles. Each role gets one or more privileges. David Ferraiolo and Rick Kuhn formalized it in 1992. The NIST model became the standard ANSI/INCITS 359-2004.

RBAC is easy to audit. You can list who has the "admin" role. Its weak spot is per-object rules. A role applies to every object. To share one doc with one person, you need a narrow new role. Many small, one-off roles pile up. This is often called "role explosion". NIST SP 800-162 describes it for rules that depend on context.
OWASP adds a practical problem. With many roles, code fills up with checks like
hasAnyRole("SUPERUSER", "ADMIN", "ACCT_MANAGER")
. It is easy to miss one.
ABAC: rules over attributes
NIST SP 800-162 defines ABAC as allowing or denying each request based on attributes of the subject and the object, environment conditions, and a set of policies.
An attribute is a name-value pair, like
department=finance
or
time=21:00
NIST splits the work into parts. The
policy enforcement point
sits in your app and blocks or allows. The
policy decision point
evaluates the rules and returns the answer.
ABAC is flexible, but it has a real cost. "Who can see this file?" becomes a hard question. NIST says it may mean simulating the request for every known subject.
Auditors often ask exactly that question.
ReBAC and Zanzibar
Google built one authorization system, Zanzibar, for hundreds of services, including Drive, Calendar and YouTube.
It stores permissions as
relation tuples
object#relation@user
. For example,
doc:readme#owner@10
means user 10 owns doc:readme.
A user in a tuple can also be a set, such as "members of group:eng". So groups can contain groups.
A schema adds rules. One rule says "all owners are editors, and all editors are viewers". Another says viewers of the parent folder are viewers of the doc.
A check asks: "Does user U have relation R to object O?"
Step through one check. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys.
Zanzibar also had to solve the
"new enemy" problem
. The paper gives two examples.
Alice removes Bob from a folder's ACL. Then Charlie moves new documents into it. Bob must not see them. He may, if the check ignores the order of the two ACL changes.
Alice removes Bob from a document's ACL. Then Charlie adds new content. Bob must not see it. He may, if the check uses a stale ACL from before his removal.
The fix is a consistency token called a
zookie

. When content is about to be saved, the client sends a content-change check. If it is allowed, the response holds a zookie, and the client stores it with that content version. Later checks send the zookie. The check snapshot must then be "at least as fresh" as it.
This is still fast. Zanzibar answers more than 95% of checks within 10 milliseconds. It
caches
results and merges duplicate requests.
See
Caching and cache stampedes
for the same ideas.
One rule, two models
Take a docs app. Docs have an owner, editors and viewers. Docs live in shared folders. Org admins may edit every doc in their org.
In RBAC, the rule looks like this:
This is simple, but it cannot say "Asha may edit this one doc". In ReBAC, the same rules live in a schema. Here it is in OpenFGA's language:

blocks.v:
model
  schema 1.1

type user

type org
  relations
    define admin: [user]

type group
  relations
    define member: [user, group#member]

type folder
  relations
    define parent: [folder]
    define editor: [user, group#member] or editor from parent
    define viewer: [user, group#member] or editor or viewer from parent

type doc
  relations
    define org: [org]
    define parent: [folder]
    define owner: [user]
    define editor: [user, group#member] or owner or editor from parent or admin from org
    define viewer: [user, group#member] or editor or viewer from parent

c.v: Each doc also needs a tuple that links it to its org, like
doc:plan#org@org:acme
. Without it, the admin rule never matches.
Sharing a doc is now one tuple, like
doc:plan#editor@user:asha
. No new role. The app asks one question:
Where to enforce
Check on the server, on every request. OWASP says to deny by default and never trust checks on the client.
The check must be for the exact object. Missing it is
broken object level authorization
(BOLA). OWASP calls it "extremely common in API-based applications".
The npm bug adds one more rule. The check and the action must use the same object ID, from the same source.
Load the object once, check it, then act on that loaded object.
A gateway can check tokens. Object checks need your data, so they belong in the service. See
API gateways and edge concerns
. Put the check behind one interface, so the domain code does not care which engine answers. See
Clean and hexagonal architecture
Policy engines and permission services
A
policy engine
keeps rules apart from app code. Your code sends a question with JSON input and gets a decision back.
OPA
is a general-purpose engine. Policies are written in a language called Rego.
Cedar
uses
permit
and
forbid
policies. If no policy matches, the answer is deny. One matching
forbid
beats any
permit
OpenFGA
and
SpiceDB
are not policy engines in this sense. They are open source permission services inspired by Zanzibar. They store the relationships and answer checks.
Keep policies in Git, reviewed like code. Pick a tool for your model, not for its marketing page.
Checking versus listing
"May Asha open doc:plan?" is one check. "Show me every doc Asha can see" is a different problem. Checking each doc one by one is too slow.
OpenFGA's ListObjects API answers it, but its docs aim it at small collections. It has a time limit and a maximum number of results.
Zanzibar offers an Expand API, which returns the tree of users and groups behind a relation. Google's clients use it to build search indexes that respect access.
Tenants, tests and audits
In a
multi-tenant
app, every query and every object ID must carry the
tenant
. Never let a tuple or a role from tenant A match an object in tenant B. See
Multi-tenancy and noisy neighbours
Write unit and
integration tests
for authorization logic. Log decisions, but not too much and not too little.
RBAC
List the role's members.
Needs a role per object.
Role explosion.
Staff tools and admin panels with a few fixed jobs.
ABAC
May need a simulation per subject.
, through attributes like
owner
Hard to audit and to debug.
Rules depend on time, place, data labels or training.
ReBAC (Zanzibar style)
Expand or list the relation.
One tuple per share.
A new store to run and keep in sync.
Sharing, folders, teams and nested groups.
Policy engine on top
Depends on the model inside.
Depends.
Another service in the request path.
Many services must apply the same rules.
Simple rule:
start with a few roles. Add relationships when users start sharing things. Add attributes only for rules that truly depend on context.

sections.title: At work: how a senior uses this

c.v: Before you add a role, ask:
"Is this really a relationship, like owner or member?"
In code review, ask:
"Is the object we check the same object we change?"
Keep one
authorize(user, action, object)
entry point. Ban role checks scattered in handlers.
Write a permission matrix test: for each role or relationship, try each action, and expect allow or deny.
Prepare for the auditor's question, "Who can see customer X's data?", before they ask.
Plan for removal. When someone leaves a team, how fast does access end everywhere?
Load-test the check path. It runs on every request.
"Find every place in this repo that checks a role or permission. Group them by resource, and show any handler that reads or writes an object without a check."
"For each endpoint that takes an object ID, show where the ID used for the authorization check comes from, and where the ID used for the write comes from. Flag any that differ."
"Write an OpenFGA model for this app: users, groups, folders with parents, docs, and org admins. Then write tests for owner, shared folder, removed member and other-tenant cases."
The check runs on the server and denies by default.
The check and the action use the same loaded object, not two copies of the request.
Every query and tuple includes the tenant.
Removing a user from a group removes their access in a test.
Listing pages filter by permission, not only by a hidden button.
The AI did not invent APIs. Compare its calls with the engine's docs.

q.v: Your docs app has roles "viewer", "editor" and "admin". A customer wants to share one doc with one outside person. What happens if you only use RBAC?

options.v: Nothing changes. Give the person the "viewer" role.
You need a new role per doc, or the person can view every doc. Roles start to multiply.
RBAC cannot store outside users at all.

why.v: A role applies to every object. Sharing one object needs a narrow role per object. This is often called "role explosion".

q.v: Which question is hardest to answer in a pure ABAC system?

options.v: May this user read this file right now?
Which attributes does this request carry?

why.v: NIST SP 800-162 says finding every subject with access to one object may mean simulating the request for every known subject.

q.v: In Zanzibar, Alice removes Bob from a doc's ACL, then adds secret text. What stops a check from using the old ACL for the new text?

options.v: The zookie stored with the content version. Checks for it run on a snapshot at least as fresh.

why.v: The client stores a zookie with each content change and sends it with later checks. The check snapshot must be at least as fresh as that zookie.

q.v: In the npm bug, the authorization service checked the package in the URL. The publisher used the package inside the uploaded file. What is the lesson?

options.v: Move the check to the client.
Check permission on the exact object the action will change, using the same data.

why.v: The check passed for one package, and the write happened to another. GitHub fixed it by making both services use the same package.
